title: Gangs of New York
full_review:
After showing his sensitive side with such films as "The Age of Innocence" and "Kundun," director Martin Scorsese returns to his more customary extreme violence with the brutally vicious "Gangs of New York" (Miramax). It's not a pretty sight, and it would be surprising if it is embraced by a mass audience.

Disturbingly, from the opening scene, murderous violence is linked to religious faith as if one honors God by killing those who oppose you. And there is much strife in the crime-drenched Five Points section of 1846 New York City, where waves of Irish immigrants have raised the hateful ire of nativist gang leader Bill the Butcher Cutter (Daniel Day-Lewis), and a mass showdown is in the offing. Meanwhile, his brawny nemesis, Irish gang leader Priest Vallon (Liam Neeson), prays and gives his little son Amsterdam a medal, teaching him about killing -- before he himself is killed as his son watches the gleeful Cutter stab him deeply and with relish.

Young Vallon is put in reform school and doesn't return to the Five Points until 1862, a grown man (Leonardo DiCaprio) unrecognized by most. But he's still wearing the medal, and the hate that burns inside him blends right in with those around him who are all thieves, killers or corrupt politicians -- and Cutter is king. Vallon works his way into Cutter's good graces, saving his life at one point but all the while plotting his bloody demise.

Woven into this ragged tapestry is a romantic triangle, in which Vallon's childhood buddy, Johnny (Henry Thomas), keeps his identity secret until he sees the thief he loves, Jenny (Cameron Diaz), in Vallon's carnal embrace.

Once exposed, the crafty Vallon re-energizes the immigrant gangs for a repeat of the original street battle against the gangs that took his father's life. However, swirling around Cutter and Vallon's imminent face-off are New York City's Civil War Draft Riots that are engulfing the city in bloodshed.

From the excruciatingly long opening street fight where the snow turns red from all the bludgeoning, hacking and clubbing, grisly excess is at the core of the film. So much so that the historical context disappears into the background until the final climactic bloodbath. Though Scorsese strives for an epic tale, the characters lack the necessary richness and depth for us to care about. Their personal stories of greed and vengeance overwhelm the broader canvas of impoverished immigrants trying to survive on the tip of Manhattan as the Civil War rages.

The period visuals are meticulous to the point of being overdone, with no shortage of crowd scenes of filthy children, topless prostitutes and teeming mobs armed with hatchets, razors, knives, and all other manner of killing instruments. Nor are the brutal fight scenes well-shot, or even edited for coherence. And for a master director with a $100 million budget, the obvious presence of an overhead boom microphone in one scene is incredible.

With all the characters so vicious, the story has little emotional resonance. Even knife-wielding Jenny is a fierce hellion whose transformation into a gushy nursemaid after Vallon is injured is unconvincing.

Despite the film's belabored ultra-realism, it fails to be dramatically stirring. Instead of a story about the immigrant experience in 19th-century New York, it seems more about butchery for its own sake and the love of slaughter. We are not even sure why the gangs are fighting; we are just led to believe it's some sort of virtuous revolt since the killers all seemed filled with religious fervor. It is this nasty pairing of prayer and hate-filled bloodletting that is especially repugnant.

At nearly three hours, this vision of old New York is more poisonous than powerful.

Due to excessive graphic violence linked to religious zeal, a sexual encounter, extended bordello nudity, brief drug abuse, racial epithets, intermittent rough language and recurring profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
